patient.name: Kwame Mensah
patient.complaint: Sudden severe left testicular pain that woke him at 5 am
background: Year 10 student in Tottenham, plays Sunday league football
Two weeks ago: 20 minutes of left testicular pain that settled by itself
No medical history, no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young male, sudden testicular pain, a high-riding testis and an absent cremasteric reflex. Epididymo-orchitis is the classic distractor.

points: Kwame, 15, woken at **5 am** by severe left testicular pain.
Vomited twice in the ambulance; also aches low in his tummy.
No injury. Mum says he looks grey.
It is now **8 am**: 3 hours since onset.

steps.lead: Kwame's cord has likely twisted and cut off his testis's blood supply. The clock started at 5 am: the **6-hour** window is what drives everything.

visual.title: Hours since pain started
visual.label: Kwame 3 h
visual.caption: Kwame is inside the 6-hour window. Every hour on the way to theatre counts.

steps.text: Always ask the exact time the pain started.

steps.lead: Kwame is the peak age, and his **20-minute episode two weeks ago** was probably intermittent torsion that untwisted itself.
Sudden pain, vomiting and lower abdominal pain without trauma: Kwame has the full classic history.

visual.title: Where Kwame also feels pain
visual.caption: Testicular pain is often referred to the lower abdomen. Always examine the testes in a boy with abdominal pain.

points: Left testis sits **higher** than the right, with a **horizontal lie**.
Stroking the inner left thigh: **no cremasteric reflex** on the left.
Lifting the testis does **not** ease the pain.

steps.lead: High-riding, horizontal lie, absent cremasteric reflex and a **positive Prehn's sign**: Kwame's examination is textbook torsion.

steps.q: Kwame's left cremasteric reflex is absent. Why?
o: The genitofemoral nerve runs in the twisted cord
steps.r: The reflex arc (femoral branch afferent, genital branch efferent of the **genitofemoral nerve**) runs through the spermatic cord, which is torted.

steps.lead: If Kwame waits, the testis infarcts. Later he could face **atrophy** and reduced fertility.

steps.title: Torsion vs epididymo-orchitis
head: Feature
Torsion
Epididymo-orchitis
rows: Sexually active adult or older man

steps.lead: Kwame's dipstick is clear. That fits torsion and makes **epididymo-orchitis** much less likely.

steps.text: Prehn's sign is **not reliable enough** to rule torsion out. If torsion is possible, the boy goes to theatre.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate next step?' where the answer is urgent surgical exploration, not an ultrasound. If a Doppler is mentioned, it shows reduced or absent flow.

steps.q: The registrar asks what confirms Kwame's diagnosis. What is the gold standard?
steps.r: **Surgical exploration** confirms and treats torsion at the same time. It is a clinical diagnosis.

steps.lead: Kwame's history and examination are enough. He goes straight to theatre; nobody books a scan first.

steps.title: Bedside tests in ED
steps.text: A normal dipstick supports torsion. It is quick, but it must never hold up theatre.

steps.lead: If Kwame's story had been unclear, a **Doppler** could show reduced flow. Here it would only waste ischaemic time.

steps.title: Suspected torsion: the pathway
nodes: Sudden testicular pain in a young male
Clinical signs: high-riding, absent cremasteric reflex
steps.caption: Imaging is not a step on this pathway when torsion is clinically suspected.

visual.title: Testicular salvage by time to surgery (approximate)
visual.caption: Salvage falls sharply after 6 hours. A scan that takes an hour costs testes.

steps.text: A **normal Doppler** does not exclude torsion (intermittent or partial twists). Clinical suspicion still means exploration.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': emergency surgical exploration with bilateral orchidopexy. Variants: GP sees the boy (urgent transfer) or the testis is dead (orchidectomy).

steps.q: Kwame is 3 hours into his pain. What happens now?
o: Analgesia and review in the morning
steps.r: He goes to theatre for **emergency exploration**. Analgesia is given, but nothing delays surgery.

steps.lead: Kwame is consented and taken to theatre within the hour. Any delay risks **irreversible infarction**.
In theatre the left testis is untwisted. **Both** testes are fixed, because Kwame's Bell-Clapper anatomy is almost certainly on both sides.

steps.title: In theatre
nodes: Warm and wait: does colour return?
steps.caption: The other testis is fixed whatever happens to the torted one.

steps.lead: Kwame's testis pinked up, so it was kept. Had it stayed black, an **orchidectomy** would have been done.

steps.text: If a GP sees suspected torsion, the answer is **urgent transfer to hospital** (same-day surgical team), not a referral letter or a scan.
Do not pick 'antibiotics' because he is young and has a swollen testis. Antibiotics treat epididymo-orchitis; torsion needs a surgeon.

science.exam: Expect applied anatomy and physiology: why the Bell-Clapper deformity allows rotation, why veins block before arteries, and why the other testis is fixed.

steps.lead: At surgery Kwame's tunica vaginalis wrapped high around the cord, so the testis hung free like a clapper inside a bell.

steps.title: Why the testis dies
steps.caption: Venous outflow fails before arterial inflow.

steps.lead: Kwame's swollen, tense testis is the **venous congestion** stage. Arterial inflow fails next.
Kwame reached theatre at about 4 hours, inside the window, which is why his testis survived.

steps.q: Kwame's mum asks why they operated on his healthy right side too. What is the reason?
o: The Bell-Clapper deformity is usually bilateral
steps.r: The anatomical fault is usually on **both sides**, so the untwisted testis is at future risk.

steps.lead: Fixing Kwame's right testis now prevents a future torsion on the side he still relies on.

steps.text: Absent cremasteric reflex: the **genitofemoral nerve** (L1–L2) carries both limbs of the reflex through the spermatic cord.

mcq.q: What is the main anatomical risk factor for testicular torsion?
mcq.r: The **Bell-Clapper deformity** lets the testis hang freely and rotate.

mcq.q: Which reflex is typically absent in testicular torsion?
mcq.r: The **cremasteric reflex** arc runs in the spermatic cord, which is twisted.

mcq.q: What does a positive Prehn's sign mean in torsion?
o: Pain is not relieved by elevation
mcq.r: In torsion, lifting the testis does **not** relieve pain; in epididymitis it often does.

mcq.q: Which bedside test best helps separate torsion from epididymo-orchitis?
mcq.r: The **urine dipstick** is typically normal in torsion but shows infection markers in epididymo-orchitis.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for testicular torsion?
mcq.r: **Surgical exploration**; torsion is a clinical diagnosis and surgery is never delayed for imaging.

mcq.q: If a Doppler ultrasound is done, what does it typically show in torsion?
What is the first-line management of testicular torsion?
At exploration the testis is non-viable. What is done?
mcq.r: A dead testis is removed (**orchidectomy**) and the other side is fixed.

mcq.q: Which vessels are occluded first when the cord twists?
mcq.r: **Venous outflow** blocks first, causing congestion and oedema that then compromise arterial inflow.

mcq.q: Why is orchidopexy performed on both sides?
mcq.r: The predisposing **Bell-Clapper** anatomy is usually bilateral.

technique.stem: A 14 year old boy has a 2 hour history of sudden severe right testicular pain that started while he was sitting in class. He has vomited once. He had a similar short-lived pain a month ago. His right testis lies higher than the left with a horizontal lie, and the right cremasteric reflex is absent.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis question about acute scrotal pain: think torsion first in any young male.

clues: similar short-lived pain a month ago
higher than the left with a horizontal lie
steps.x: Adolescent, sudden onset, previous intermittent episode, high-riding horizontal testis and absent reflex: every clue points one way.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sudden pain plus a high-riding testis with no cremasteric reflex: **testicular torsion**.

elim: Epididymo-orchitis is gradual, in sexually active men, with a positive dipstick and a present reflex.
A hernia gives a groin lump that may reduce, not a high-riding testis.
Tumours are usually painless, hard lumps in men 20 to 45.
Varicocele is a dull ache and a 'bag of worms', not sudden severe pain.

steps.x: **C. Testicular torsion.** Rule: sudden pain + high-riding testis + absent cremasteric reflex = torsion until proven otherwise.

technique.stem: A 16 year old boy has a 3 hour history of sudden severe left testicular pain and nausea. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. The left testis is high-riding and very tender. Elevating it does not relieve the pain. A urine dipstick is negative.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?

steps.x: 'Next step' in suspected torsion: is this a test or a treatment? Here the test IS the operation.
Clinically obvious torsion inside the 6-hour window, negative Prehn's (no relief) and clear dipstick.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis. Gold standard and treatment: **urgent surgical exploration**.

elim: CT has no role and wastes ischaemic time.
Urine culture is for infection; the dipstick is already clear.
Doppler may show reduced flow but must **never delay** surgery when torsion is suspected.
Tumour markers are for a painless testicular lump.

steps.x: **E. Urgent surgical exploration.** Rule: suspected torsion goes to theatre, not to the scanner.

technique.stem: A 13 year old boy has a 4 hour history of sudden left testicular pain. He is seen by his GP. His left testis is high and tender with an absent cremasteric reflex. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oral ciprofloxacin and review in 48 hours
Urgently transfer to hospital for surgical exploration

steps.x: Initial management in primary care: what does this boy need first?
Torsion with 2 hours left in the window, seen outside hospital.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First step is **urgent transfer to hospital** for emergency exploration and bilateral orchidopexy.

elim: Antibiotics treat epididymo-orchitis; torsion needs surgery.
Waiting until tomorrow means the testis will infarct.
Outpatient imaging delays surgery by days.
A routine referral is far too slow for a surgical emergency.

steps.x: **E. Urgent transfer.** Rule: torsion is a surgical emergency wherever the patient is seen.

technique.stem: A 15 year old boy undergoes emergency scrotal exploration for a left testicular torsion. The surgeon notes that the tunica vaginalis is attached abnormally high on the spermatic cord on both sides. After untwisting the left testis, both testes are fixed.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason the right testis is fixed?
o: It reduces the risk of testicular cancer
The predisposing anatomy is usually bilateral
The right testis is already ischaemic

steps.x: Applied anatomy: why fix a testis that never twisted?

clues: tunica vaginalis is attached abnormally high
steps.x: High investment of the tunica vaginalis is the **Bell-Clapper deformity**, described here on both sides.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The Bell-Clapper deformity is usually bilateral, so the other testis is at future risk.

elim: Orchidopexy does not change cancer risk.
No hydrocele is described.
The right testis never twisted, so it is not ischaemic.
Fixation does not improve sperm production.

steps.x: **C. The predisposing anatomy is usually bilateral.** Rule: one torsion = fix both sides.

practice.stem: A 17 year old boy has a 1 hour history of sudden severe right testicular pain that woke him from sleep. He has vomited twice and has lower abdominal pain. He has had no injury. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. The right testis is swollen, very tender and lies higher than the left.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden testicular pain with vomiting and a high-riding testis in a teenager is torsion. Lower abdominal pain is a referred symptom, not a sign of appendicitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a young male with acute scrotal pain.
Sudden pain, often waking the boy, with vomiting, no trauma and a high-riding testis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Testicular torsion.**

elim: Appendicitis gives abdominal pain but a normal testis.
Epididymo-orchitis is gradual with a normally sited testis.
A hernia gives a groin lump, not a high-riding testis.
There was no injury.

steps.x: **D. Testicular torsion.** Lower abdominal pain is common in torsion: always examine the testes.

practice.stem: A 25 year old man has a 3 day history of gradually worsening left scrotal pain and burning on passing urine. He has a new sexual partner. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. The left testis lies normally. Elevating it eases the pain. The cremasteric reflex is present.
practice.q: Which feature in this history makes testicular torsion least likely?
practice.e: Torsion presents with sudden-onset pain. Gradual pain, fever, dysuria, relief on elevation and a present cremasteric reflex fit epididymo-orchitis instead.

steps.x: This asks which feature argues against torsion: think about the signature symptom.
Torsion's signature symptom is **sudden onset**. Gradual pain, relief on elevation and a present reflex point away.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **gradual onset** is the strongest feature against torsion.

elim: Torsion peaks in adolescents but can occur in young men.
Torsion can affect either side.
Tachycardia occurs with pain in either condition.
Both conditions cause a tender scrotum.

steps.x: **B. Gradual onset.** Rule: torsion is sudden; days of build-up suggest epididymo-orchitis.

practice.stem: A 14 year old boy has sudden onset left testicular pain for 2 hours. His pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 120/70 mmHg. On examination the left testis is tender. The doctor strokes the upper inner aspect of his left thigh.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the left?
practice.e: The cremasteric reflex is absent in torsion because both limbs of the reflex arc (genitofemoral nerve) run through the twisted spermatic cord.

steps.x: Most likely examination finding: which sign is the doctor testing?

clues: strokes the upper inner aspect of his left thigh
steps.x: Stroking the inner thigh tests the **cremasteric reflex**. Sudden pain in a teenager means torsion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: In torsion the cremasteric reflex is **absent**.

elim: A brisk reflex makes torsion less likely.
Pain relief on elevation suggests epididymitis; torsion has a positive Prehn's sign.
Babinski tests the plantar response, not the scrotum.
Transillumination suggests a hydrocele or cyst.

steps.x: **A. Absent cremasteric reflex.** The genitofemoral nerve runs in the twisted cord.

practice.stem: A 13 year old boy is having emergency surgery for a right testicular torsion. He had two brief self-resolving episodes of right testicular pain in the past month. The surgeon finds the testis hanging freely within the tunica vaginalis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely predisposing factor?
practice.e: The Bell-Clapper deformity leaves the testis unanchored to the tunica vaginalis so it can rotate. Previous intermittent episodes are a recognised warning sign.

steps.x: Most likely cause: which anatomical fault lets a testis twist?

clues: hanging freely within the tunica vaginalis
steps.x: A freely hanging testis is the **Bell-Clapper deformity**; the earlier episodes were intermittent torsion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bell-Clapper deformity.**

elim: Undescended testis is a risk for cancer and infertility, not this finding.
Mumps causes orchitis, not a free-hanging testis.
Microlithiasis is an ultrasound finding linked to tumours.
A varicocele is dilated veins, not abnormal fixation.

steps.x: **A. Bell-Clapper deformity.** Previous intermittent pain is also a risk factor.

practice.stem: A 16 year old boy has a 3 hour history of sudden left testicular pain. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. The doctor gently lifts the left testis towards the inguinal canal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely response?
o: Pain moves to the right testis
Testis drops to a lower position
practice.e: In torsion, Prehn's sign is present: pain is not relieved by elevating the testis. Relief on elevation favours epididymo-orchitis.

steps.x: Most likely finding: lifting the testis is Prehn's sign.
Sudden pain in a teenager means torsion. In torsion, elevation does not help.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **No relief of pain**: a positive Prehn's sign.

elim: Relief on elevation suggests epididymitis.
Pain does not move to the other side.
Coughing tests for a hernia, and does not relieve pain.
A torted testis is held high by the shortened cord.

steps.x: **B. No relief of pain.** Prehn's sign present = pain not relieved by elevation.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man has had severe right testicular pain for 30 hours. He was too embarrassed to come in earlier. The right testis is high-riding, firm and discoloured, with an absent cremasteric reflex.
practice.q: Which is the most likely outcome if surgery is not performed?
practice.e: Delayed treatment leads to testicular infarction/necrosis, later atrophy and possible infertility. Salvage falls sharply after 6 hours.

steps.x: Most likely complication: what happens to an untreated torted testis?
Torsion far outside the 6-hour window, with a discoloured testis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Testicular infarction**, then atrophy.

elim: Ischaemia beyond 6 hours rarely recovers.
A hydrocele is a fluid collection, not ischaemia.
Torsion does not cause seminoma.
Varicocele is unrelated to torsion.

steps.x: **D. Testicular infarction.** Delay leads to necrosis, atrophy and reduced fertility.

practice.stem: A 15 year old boy has a 2 hour history of sudden severe right testicular pain and vomiting. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. The right testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and an absent cremasteric reflex.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis: **surgical exploration** is the gold standard.

practice.stem: A 20 year old man has a 5 hour history of left scrotal pain that began suddenly but has partly eased. Examination is equivocal. A urine dipstick is negative. A scrotal Doppler ultrasound is performed while theatre is being prepared.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the left?

Normal flow with a hypoechoic mass
Reduced blood flow to the testis
Simple cyst in the epididymal head
Tortuous dilated veins above the testis
practice.e: Doppler in torsion shows reduced (or absent) flow. Increased flow is the pattern in epididymo-orchitis.

steps.x: Most likely imaging finding: what does torsion do to blood flow?
Sudden onset and a clean dipstick point to torsion. Torsion cuts off the supply.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reduced blood flow** to the affected testis.

elim: Increased flow suggests epididymo-orchitis.
A hypoechoic mass suggests a tumour.

practice.stem: A 14 year old boy has a 2 hour history of sudden severe left testicular pain. He is in the Emergency Department. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 124/70 mmHg. The left testis is high-riding with an absent cremasteric reflex. Urine dipstick is negative.

practice.stem: A 16 year old boy has emergency scrotal exploration for right testicular torsion after 26 hours of pain. After untwisting and warming, the right testis remains black and does not bleed when incised.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Fix the right testis and leave the left alone
Leave both testes unfixed and give antibiotics
Right orchidopexy and review in clinic
practice.e: A non-viable testis is removed. The contralateral testis is still fixed because the Bell-Clapper deformity is usually bilateral.

steps.x: Management at surgery: is the testis viable, and what about the other side?
Late presentation and a black, non-bleeding testis: it is **non-viable**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Remove it (**orchidectomy**) and fix the other side (**orchidopexy**).

Antibiotics do not treat infarction.

steps.x: **C. Right orchidectomy and left orchidopexy.**

practice.stem: A 15 year old boy has sudden left testicular pain for 90 minutes. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 126/76 mmHg. Clinical findings suggest torsion. The urology registrar is on the way. The ED doctor considers what to do while waiting.

Send urine for culture and await the result

steps.x: Suspected torsion early in the window: every minute counts.

practice.stem: A 14 year old boy has a 4 hour history of left testicular torsion. At surgery the testis is swollen, dark and congested, but its arterial pulsation is still present.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the swelling at this stage?

steps.x: Low-pressure **venous outflow** blocks first; oedema then compromises the arteries.

steps.x: **E. Venous outflow occluded before arterial inflow.**

glossary.torsion: Twisting of an organ on its blood supply; here the testis rotating on its spermatic cord.
glossary.spermatic cord: Bundle carrying the testicular artery, veins, vas deferens and nerves from the groin to the testis.
glossary.tunica vaginalis: Double layer of membrane surrounding the front and sides of the testis.
glossary.Bell-Clapper deformity: Abnormally high attachment of the tunica vaginalis, so the testis hangs freely and can rotate.
glossary.cremasteric reflex: Stroking the inner thigh makes the cremaster muscle lift the testis on that side.
glossary.cremaster: Thin muscle around the spermatic cord that raises the testis.
glossary.genitofemoral nerve: L1 to L2 nerve whose branches carry both limbs of the cremasteric reflex.
glossary.Prehn's sign: Pain not relieved by lifting the testis; present in torsion, relief suggests epididymitis.
glossary.high-riding: Testis sitting higher in the scrotum than the other side because the twisted cord is shorter.
glossary.horizontal lie: Testis lying sideways rather than vertically, typical of Bell-Clapper anatomy.
glossary.epididymo-orchitis: Infection and inflammation of the epididymis and testis, with gradual pain and a positive dipstick.
glossary.orchidopexy: Surgical fixation of the testis to the scrotal wall so it cannot twist.
glossary.surgical exploration: Opening the scrotum in theatre to look at, untwist and assess the testis.
glossary.Doppler: Ultrasound technique showing blood flow; flow is reduced in torsion.
glossary.ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to tissue, causing damage if prolonged.
glossary.infarction: Death of tissue from loss of blood supply.
glossary.atrophy: Shrinking of an organ, here a testis after ischaemic damage.
glossary.intermittent torsion: Brief episodes of twisting that untwist by themselves; a warning sign of full torsion.
glossary.urine dipstick: Bedside urine test for leucocytes, nitrites and blood; normal in torsion.
glossary.nitrites: Dipstick marker of bacteria in urine, pointing to infection rather than torsion.
glossary.leucocytes: White cells; positive on dipstick in infection such as epididymo-orchitis.
glossary.venous congestion: Blood pooling because outflow is blocked; causes swelling in early torsion.
glossary.viable: Still alive and able to recover once the blood supply returns.
glossary.varicocele: Dilated veins above the testis, feeling like a 'bag of worms'.
glossary.hydrocele: Fluid around the testis that transilluminates; usually painless.
glossary.transilluminates: Lets light shine through, as fluid-filled swellings do.
glossary.referred pain: Pain felt away from its source, such as testicular pain felt in the lower abdomen.
glossary.salvage: Saving the testis so it can be kept rather than removed.
